'''''Avena sterilis''''' ('''animated oat''', '''sterile oat''', '''wild oat''', '''wild red oat''', '''winter wild oat'''; [[syn.]] ''Avena ludoviciana'' Durieu; ''Avena macrocarpa'' Moench;<ref name="BMPW"/> '''''Avena sterilis'' ssp. ''sterilis''''';<ref name="BMPW"/> '''''Avena sterilis'' ssp. ''ludoviciana''''') is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] weed whose seeds are edible. Many common names of this plant refer to the movement of its [[panicle]] in the wind.<ref name="CABI"/>

==Description==
===Appearance===
''Avena sterilis'' is a stout, broad-leaved grass that grows up to {{convert|1.5|m|abbr=on}} tall. At maturity, it has leaf blades that are up to {{convert|60|cm|abbr=on}} long, and {{convert|6-14|mm|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name="CABI">{{cite journal |title=''Avena sterilis'' (winter wild oat) |journal=[[CABI Compendium]]|publisher=[[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International|CABI]]|page=8062 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.8062 |date=7 January 2022|volume=<!---->|s2cid=253604348 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[File:Avena sterilis florets.jpg|left|thumb|[[Floret]]s]]
It has an [[inflorescence]] that is either an equilateral or a slightly one-sided panicle. The [[spikelets]] usually have 3 [[florets]],<ref name="BMPW"/> but can have anywhere from 2 to 5.<ref name="CABI"/> The spikelets (without [[Awn_(botany)|awns]]) are {{convert|1.7-4.5|cm|abbr=on}} long; the [[glumes]] are {{convert|2.4-5|cm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="BMPW"/> 

The florets can either be a straw yellow or slightly reddish in colour. Occasionally, there can be reddish hairs at the base of the floret.<ref name="ICSI"/>

The [[Spikelet#Lemma|lemma]] is usually {{convert|1.5-4|cm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="BMPW"/>  The florets are elongate and taper at the top. The two florets closest to the glumes have a twisted dorsal awn that is {{convert|3-9|cm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="BMPW"/><ref name="ICSI">{{cite web |title=Weed Seed: Avena sterilis (Sterile oat) |website=[[Canadian Food Inspection Agency]], Seeds Identification |date=7 November 2017 |publisher=Government of Canada |url=https://inspection.canada.ca/plant-health/seeds/seed-testing-and-grading/seeds-identification/avena-sterilis/eng/1473681944310/1473681944839 |access-date=10 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220817221725/https://inspection.canada.ca/plant-health/seeds/seed-testing-and-grading/seeds-identification/avena-sterilis/eng/1473681944310/1473681944839 |archive-date=17 August 2022}}</ref>

===Varieties and subspecies===
One can distinguish between the two subspecies, ''A. sterilis sterilis'' and ''A. sterilis ludoviciana'', using the size of the reproductive parts of the flower.<ref name="BMPW"/>

A study of 139 populations of ''A. sterilis L.'' in Spain revealed 6 varieties based on morphological classifications, though no new subspecies were formally described.<ref name="GBDM">{{cite journal |last1=Garcia-Baudin |first1=J. M. |last2=Hsalto |first2=T. |last3=Aguirre |first3=R. |title=Differentes types morphologiques chez ''Avena sterilis'' L.|journal=[[Fragmenta Herbologica Jugoslavica]]|date=1981 |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=57–71|trans-title=Different morphological types of ''Avena sterilis'' L.}}</ref>

===Reproduction===
''A. sterilis'' is [[hexaploid]].<ref name="PGDO"/> It is an [[annual plant]],<ref name="CABI"/><ref name="PFAF">{{cite web |title=Avena sterilis L. |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Avena_sterilis |website=Plants for a Future Database |publisher=[[Plants for a Future]] |access-date=10 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230510235440/https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Avena_sterilis |archive-date=10 May 2023}}</ref> with a life cycle that mirrors many [[cereal]] crops.<ref name="ICSI"/> While an individual plant is capable of producing as many as 200 seeds, the average seed production of a single plant is 13-21 seeds.<ref name="ICSI"/> Seeds regularly live in the soil for upwards of two years, and can survive for as many as 5 years prior to [[germination]].<ref name="ICSI"/><ref name="BMPW">{{cite book |last1=Tidemann |first1=Breanne D. |last2=Geddes |first2=Charles M. |last3=Beckie |first3=Hugh J. |editor1-last=Chauhan |editor1-first=Bhagirath Singh |title=Biology and Management of Problematic Crop Weed Species |date=2021 |publisher=[[Academic Press]]|chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B978012822917000015X |isbn=978-0-12-822917-0 |pages=43–66 |access-date=11 May 2023 |chapter=3}}</ref>

===Distribution===
''A. sterilis'' is native to the [[Mediterranean Basin]] and [[Western Asia|West]], [[Central Asia|Central]] and [[South Asia|South]] Asia, but is widely naturalized elsewhere.<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" /> The species grows on all continents except Antarctica.<ref name="ICSI"/>

In [[North America]], it grows as an introduced species in the U.S. states of California, Oregon,<ref name="USDA">{{cite web |title=Avena sterilis L. |url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=AVST |website=NRCS PLANTS Database |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]] |access-date=11 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220705131537/https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=AVST |archive-date=5 July 2022}}</ref> New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania,<ref name="ICSI"/> and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec.<ref name="USDA"/><ref name="ICSI"/>

===Pests and pathogens===
''A. sterilis'' is a host to the pathogenic nematode ''[[Ditylenchus dipsaci]]''.<ref name="nematode">{{cite journal |last1=Abbad Andaloussi |first1=F. |last2=Bachikh |first2=J. |title=Studies on the host range of ''Ditylenchus dipsaci'' in Morocco. |journal=[[Nematologia Mediterranea]]|date=2001 |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=65–67}}</ref> It is a host to the protist plant pathogen ''[[Sclerophthora macrospora]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Singh |first1=P. J. |last2=Bedi |first2=P. S. |title=New graminaceous hosts of ''Sclerophthora macrospora''|journal=[[Plant Disease Research]]|date=1991 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=65–67}}</ref> It is also a wild host to [[Petrobia| Petrobia latens]], commonly known as the brown wheat mite.<ref name="CABI"/> It is susceptible to two widespread diseases that infect ''Avena'' species, [[oat crown rust]] and [[stem rust]].<ref name="rust">{{cite journal |last1=Niekerk |first1=B. D. |last2=Pretorius |first2=Z. A. |last3=Boshoff |first3=W. H. P. |title=Pathogenic variability of ''Puccinia coronata'' f. sp. ''avenae'' and ''P. graminis'' f. sp. ''avenae'' on oat in South Africa |journal=Plant Disease |date=2001 |volume=85 |issue=10 |pages=1085–1090|doi=10.1094/PDIS.2001.85.10.1085 |pmid=30823281 }}</ref> It is also susceptible to the [[wheat dwarf virus]].<ref name="CABI"/>

==Relationship to humans==

===Ancestor of domesticated oats===

[[Genetic analysis]] has shown that ''A. sterilis'' grass indigenous to Southwest Asia, and modern Iran, Iraq, and Turkey is the progenitor of domesticated oat crops such as [[Oat|''A. sativa'']] and ''[[Avena byzantina|A. byzantina]]''.<ref name="PGDO">{{cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=X. |last2=Jellen |first2=E. N. |last3=Murphy |first3=J. P. |title=Progenitor Germplasm of Domesticated Hexaploid Oat |journal=Crop Science |date=1999 |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=1208–1214 |doi=10.2135/cropsci1999.0011183X003900040042x |url=https://acsess.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2135/cropsci1999.0011183X003900040042x# |access-date=11 May 2023|url-access=subscription }}</ref>. Its protein content may be as high as 30%.<ref>{{Cite book |title=McGraw-Hill encyclopedia of science & technology: an international reference work in twenty volumes including an index |date=2012 |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year= |isbn=978-0-07-179273-8 |edition=11th |volume=12 |location=New York, NY |pages=265}}</ref>

===Modern agricultural weed===
''A. sterilis'' produces seeds that are difficult to separate from grain.<ref name="CABI"/> Because of this, its seeds have spread around the world as a contaminant in wool, cereal grain, and seed.<ref name="CABI"/><ref name="ICSI"/>

Because it thrives in the same conditions as many agricultural crops and has similar lifecycles, the grass directly competes with and reduces yield in arable crops.<ref name="IJWS">{{cite journal |last1=Pandey |first1=A. K. |last2=Prasad |first2=K. |last3=Singh |first3=P. |last4=Singh |first4=R. D. |title=Comparative yield loss assessment and crop-weed association in major winter crops of mid hills of N-W Himalayas |journal=[[Indian Journal of Weed Science]]|date=1998 |volume=30 |issue=1,2 |pages=54–57}}</ref><ref name="CAWO">{{cite journal |last1=Walia |first1=U. S. |last2=Brar |first2=L. S. |title=Competitive ability of wild oats (''Avena ludoviciana'' Dur.) and broad leaf weeds with wheat in relation to crop density and nitrogen levels |journal=[[Indian Journal of Weed Science]]|date=2001 |volume=33 |issue=3,4 |pages=120–123}}</ref><ref name="WCEA">{{cite book |last1=Terry |first1=P. J. |title=A Guide to Weed Control in East African Crops |date=1984 |publisher=[[Kenya Literature Bureau]]|location=[[Nairobi]], Kenya |page=186}}</ref>

Castillejo-González ''et al.'', 2014 locate ''A. sterilis'' infested fields with almost perfect accuracy using [[QuickBird]] ([[satellite imagery]]) and various [[image classifier]]s.<ref>

===Herbicide resistance===
''Avena sterilis'' ssp. ''ludoviciana'' with multiple [[herbicide resistance]] - at 2 [[site of action|sites of action]] (SOAs) - was first observed in [[Kermanshah]], Khuzestan, Iran, in [[winter wheat]] cultivation in 2010.<ref name="Weed-Science-resist" /> These populations are known to be resistant to [[clodinafop-propargyl]], [[iodosulfuron-methyl-sodium]], and [[mesosulfuron-methyl]].<ref name="Weed-Science-resist" /> 

[[Resistance to fenoxaprop-P-ethyl]] in ''Asl'' (and ''[[Avena fatua|A. fatua]]'') has [[Herbicide# Resistance|evolved]] in several [[field (agriculture)|field]]s in [[England]].<ref name="Cavan-et-al-1998" /> Although these ''Asl'' and ''A. fatua'' are also hybridising, it remains unproven if this is why they both have resistance, or in which direction this has occurred.<ref name="Cavan-et-al-1998" /> 

''A. sterilis'' populations in [[Greece]] are almost all resistant to [[diclofop]] but susceptible to most other [[herbicide]]s, including others of the same [[mode of action|MOA]] (i.e., [[AACase inhibitor]]s).<ref name="Travlos-et-al-2011" /> However, most Greek populations do have diclofop resistance and ''some'' other resistance to at least ''one'' other herbicide.<ref name="Travlos-et-al-2011" />
